title: The grocer's parrot
hook: a parrot spills oil, is struck bald, and decides every bald man must have spilled oil too (Masnavi 1.247ff)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus told himself to do every act as if it were the last. Your line was as if the last. Which conversation got your whole attention? Day one hundred seventy-six.

You see someone crying in a parking lot, and you think: breakup, I've been there. Or a coworker is quiet in a meeting, and you think: they're mad, I get quiet when I'm mad. We do it all day. We look at someone else and assume that what's going on inside them is what would be going on inside us. Usually we don't even notice we've done it. Rumi's second story in the Masnavi is short, funny and a little sharp, and it's about exactly this. It stars a bird. Today, the grocer's parrot.
screen: `CRYING IN A PARKING LOT.` → `THEY MUST FEEL WHAT I'D FEEL.` → `THE GROCER'S PARROT.`

segments.voice: A grocer had a parrot. A green, clever, talking parrot that chatted with the customers and kept an eye on the shop. One day, while the grocer was out, a cat dashed after a mouse, the parrot panicked, flapped across the counter, and knocked over the bottles of rose oil. Oil everywhere. The grocer came back, saw the mess, and in his anger struck the parrot on the head. The feathers on its head fell out. It was bald. And it stopped talking. The grocer was heartbroken. He sighed, he pulled at his beard, he gave money to the poor, hoping his parrot would speak again. Days went by in silence. Then a wandering dervish walked past the shop, one of those with a completely shaved head, bald and shining. And the parrot suddenly found its voice. It called out: hey, you! How did you end up bald? Did you spill oil from a bottle too? Everyone laughed. The parrot had made a comparison, a qiyas, and it was wrong. Same bald head, entirely different story. Here's where Rumi turns. He says: don't measure the deeds of the holy by yourself. And he gives a Persian pun: sher and shir are written alike in the Persian script, yet one means lion and the other means milk. Two things can look the same on the page and be nothing alike. Rumi's worry is spiritual: people look at saints and prophets and say, they're just like us. But it works in a parking lot too. Before you decide what someone's going through, remember the parrot. Not the same bald.
screen: `A TALKING PARROT SPILLS THE OIL.` · `STRUCK BALD, IT FALLS SILENT.` · `DID YOU SPILL OIL TOO?` · `LION AND MILK, WRITTEN ALIKE.` · then, large: `NOT THE SAME BALD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: catch one wrong comparison. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you've been judging lately, a relative, a neighbor, a person in the news. Notice the story you've told about why they are the way they are. Now ask: is that their story, or mine? Imagine two or three other reasons for the same bald head. Hold them loosely. You don't have to know the real one. Just loosen the grip of your first guess. The bell holds the time.
The grocer's parrot. Struck bald for spilling oil, it decides a bald dervish must have spilled oil too: Rumi's picture of a false comparison. Today's word.
Your line: not the same bald. Today, when you're sure you know why someone is acting a certain way, say your line and think of one other reason. Day one hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: The grocer and the parrot is one of the Masnavi's short tales, and teachers use it to warn against judging others by oneself.
